claims.text: The HEA is initially a single-phase solid solution.
The HEA initially has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Prolonged mechanical loading at elevated temperature causes elemental segregation to grain boundaries.
Reduced intergranular cohesion promotes crack propagation.
Elevated temperature drives diffusion of specific elements to grain boundaries.
Mechanical stress contributes to diffusion or segregation of specific elements to grain boundaries.
Al or Cr may be sufficiently light or mobile to segregate to grain boundaries under the proposed conditions.
The proposed grain-boundary segregation facilitates intergranular fracture under stress.
Exposure at 500–700°C for 100–500 hours under tensile or cyclic stress will produce the proposed governing behavior.
After prolonged elevated-temperature loading, fracture toughness will decrease by more than 30% relative to the initial state.
After prolonged elevated-temperature loading, fracture behavior will transition from ductile to brittle.
The hypothesis applies to elevated-temperature, mechanically loaded, high-stress service such as turbine-blade or aerospace-component operation.
The proposed segregation-driven toughness loss does not apply under ambient-temperature or short-duration loading.
A controlled comparison between prolonged elevated-temperature loading and ambient-condition exposure can reveal whether segregation, toughness loss, and fracture-mode changes occur together.
Absence of significant grain-boundary segregation, or unchanged fracture toughness and fracture mode after the specified exposure, would falsify the hypothesis.
